Medieval Halloween: Soul Cakes and Bells | History for Sleep

About 1 hour 57 min · Released Fri 23 Oct 2026 · narrated slowly for sleep

Plays from YouTube, which may set cookies. Privacy

Watch on YouTube Listen on YouTube Music

Medieval Halloween history for sleep: a calm, two-hour night on All Hallows' Eve in a late-medieval English village, with soul cakes, souling, and church bells rung all night for the souls of the dead.

🌙 No mid-video ads, nothing to wake you.

The customs, bells and soul cakes are real, taken from old parish accounts and folklore records. Our village, Agnes, Wat and the ringers are imagined.

This is a quiet bedtime documentary, narrated slowly to help you relax and drift off to sleep. No loud sounds, no sudden changes and no horror: just a soft voice, slow images, and faraway bells.

A note from Dreaming Ages

This episode began with one line in a parish account book from Heybridge in Essex, 1517: eightpence paid to John Gidney of Maldon "for a new bell-rope agenste Hallowmasse". A new rope, bought because the bells would be rung through the night for the souls of the dead. We followed that rope back into the village it served.

Sources

Researched and written for this channel from these sources. Where historians disagree, the narration says so.

  • J. Nichols, Illustrations of the Manners and Expences of Antient Times (1797), Heybridge churchwardens' accounts, via J. Brand, Observations on Popular Antiquities, ed. Ellis (1849)
  • E. Morris, "Hallowmass (When the Bells Rang All Night)", The Ringing World no. 2688 (1962)
  • T. North, Church Bells of the County and City of Lincoln (1882)
  • H. B. Walters, Church Bells of England (1912)
  • C. S. Burne (ed.), Shropshire Folk-Lore (1883–86)
  • John Aubrey, Remaines of Gentilisme and Judaisme (ed. Britten, 1881)
  • Thomas Tusser, Five Hundred Points of Good Husbandry (1573)
